title: India Is Buying Oil From Venezuela, Brazil, and Angola. The Strait of Hormuz Forced the Pivot.
excerpt: With the critical shipping lane still closed three months into the US-Iran war, Indian refiners are diversifying away from the Middle East in what analysts call a structural shift.
body:
India has sharply increased crude oil purchases from Latin America and Africa as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively shut, forcing the world's third-largest oil importer into its most significant supply chain pivot in decades.

Indian refiners have ramped up imports from **Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria** in April and May to cover shortfalls caused by the three-month-old US-Iran war, according to preliminary shipping data from Kpler. Venezuela, in particular, is on track to become India's fourth-largest oil supplier in May — a dramatic rise for a country that barely registered in India's import mix a year ago.

## The Hormuz Factor

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply normally passes, has been effectively closed to major commercial shipping since the US-Israel war with Iran began on February 28. The closure has driven Brent crude to $93 a barrel and reshaped global energy trade flows overnight.

For India, which historically sourced more than 60 percent of its crude from Middle Eastern producers, the disruption has been severe. Gulf suppliers like Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE — India's traditional backbone of oil imports — have been cut off or sharply constrained by the shipping bottleneck.

The Reserve Bank of India has set an $85 per barrel oil benchmark for the current fiscal year, signaling expectations that elevated prices will persist even if a deal reopens the strait. For the next fiscal year, the RBI projects a decline to $75 — contingent on a durable peace.

## The Latin American Lifeline

Venezuela has emerged as a surprise beneficiary. India is still receiving about 1.9 million barrels per day of Russian crude — its largest non-traditional source — but the addition of Venezuelan heavy crude has given refiners a new hedge against Gulf disruptions. Brazilian and West African barrels have similarly filled gaps, with Nigerian and Angolan light crude proving popular with Indian refiners configured for those grades.

"This is less a temporary fix than a structural adjustment," a senior executive at an Indian state-run refiner told Reuters. "We cannot keep 60 percent of our supply dependent on a single chokepoint."

The diversification mirrors what India did during the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022, when it dramatically increased Russian oil purchases while Western buyers pulled back. This time, the pivot is being driven not by sanctions arbitrage but by physical supply constraints.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching from the United States, the UK, and Canada, India's oil pivot has direct economic implications. Higher crude prices feed into domestic inflation, weakening the rupee and increasing the cost of everything from cooking gas to airline tickets.

India's forex reserves have already fallen $47 billion in three months as the RBI spends billions defending the rupee. The current account deficit is expected to widen, putting pressure on remittance values — the single most direct economic link between the diaspora and India.

On the positive side, the diversification reduces India's exposure to future Gulf disruptions. If the Hormuz-dependent supply chain was India's Achilles' heel, the current crisis is forcing a correction that could prove beneficial in the long run.

## The Deal That Could Change Everything

Over the weekend, President Trump said the US was "close to a very good deal" with Iran that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has agreed not to develop or acquire nuclear weapons, Trump said, calling it a significant concession. But he sent back toughened terms to Tehran on Saturday, and Iran's lead negotiator responded that no agreement would be signed unless Iranian rights are protected.

Oil markets are watching every signal. Brent dropped 11 percent last week on peace hopes before bouncing 2.2 percent on Monday as the tougher terms became public. A finalized deal would likely send prices sharply lower, potentially by $15-20 a barrel.

Until then, India's refiners are not waiting. The pivot to Latin American and African crude is already underway, and industry executives say they intend to maintain diversified sourcing even if Hormuz reopens.

"You don't un-diversify after something like this," the refiner executive said. "The world changed."

*Sources: Reuters, Kpler shipping data, The Business Standard, RBI monetary policy documents, The Indian EYE*
author: Diaspora Desk
